> *If the hypotenuse is twice as long as the shortest leg, then the given right triangle is a ${30^\circ}$-${60^\circ}$-${90^\circ}$ triangle.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "e07c8310-fe8a-5f3e-9ff0-7cd4e93a784c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2383 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186060471 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059637 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059465 :question/id #uuid "b5f19406-37c2-569e-9c9e-b99e00234f91" :question/math-academy-id "e-3084"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4cc0e4fc-64ca-5c1b-abbe-357e930af7a4" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060087} {:db/id 17592186060291}] :knowledge-point/title "Relating the Length of the Hypotenuse to the Length Of the Shortest Side"} :step/id #uuid "a6377883-059a-5ebf-97b1-38ef2ad683fd" :step/math-academy-id 10427 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060472}} {:db/id 17592186060472 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060875 :tutorial/content "Consider the same ${30^\circ}$-${60^\circ}$-${90^\circ}$ triangle from before. Applying the Pythagorean Theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
(2x)^{2} &= x^{2} + h^{2} \\
h^{2} &= 4x^{2} - x^{2} \\
h^{2} &= 3x^{2} \\
h &= \sqrt{3}x
\end{aligned}
$$

> *In any ${30^\circ}$-${60^\circ}$-${90^\circ}$ triangle, the length of the longer leg (which is opposite the $60^\circ$ angle) is $\sqrt{3}$ times the length of the shorter leg (which is opposite the $30^\circ$ angle).*

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the nails in the population have lengths $5\,\text{cm}$ and $\text{10}\,\text{cm},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $4:1.$ Therefore, to compute the population mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $4+1=5$ nails only with the following lengths:

$$
5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm}\,10\,\text{cm}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot 5+10) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(20+10) \\  & =\frac{30}{5} \\  & =6\,\text{cm},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot {5}^{2}+{10}^{2})-{6}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(200)-36 \\  & =40-36 \\  & =4\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sample size $n=3,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}=\frac{4}{3}\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}≈1.15\,\text{cm}
$$

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the employees in the population have working hours $38\,\text{h/week}$ and $40\,\text{h/week},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $3:1.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $3+1=4$ employees only with the following working hours:

$$
38\,\text{h/week},\,38\,\text{h/week},\,38\,\text{h/week},\,40\,\text{h/week}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{4}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(3\cdot 38+40) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(114+40) \\  & =\frac{154}{4} \\  & =38.5\,\text{h/week},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(3\cdot {38}^{2}+{40}^{2})-{38.5}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(5\,932)-1\,482.25 \\  & =1\,483-1\,482.25 \\  & =0.75\,{(\text{h/week})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the population standard deviation is $\sigma =\sqrt{0.75},$ and we have that 

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{n}}.
$$

We require that the standard error is less than $0.5\,\text{h/week}.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{n}} & <0.5 \\ \sqrt{n} & >\frac{\sqrt{0.75}}{0.5} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{{0.5}^{2}}} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{0.25}} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{3} \\ n & >3.\end{aligned}
$$

\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the bushes in the population have heights $4\,\text{ft}$ and $5\,\text{ft},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $3:2.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $3+2=5$ bushes only with the following heights:

$$
4\,\text{ft},\,4\,\text{ft},\,4\,\text{ft},\,5\,\text{ft},\,5\,\text{ft}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\cdot 4+2\cdot 5) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(12+10) \\  & =\frac{22}{5} \\  & =4.4\,\text{ft},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\cdot {4}^{2}+2\cdot {5}^{2})-{4.4}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(98)-19.36 \\  & =19.6-19.36 \\  & =0.24\,{\text{ft}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the population standard deviation is $\sigma =\sqrt{0.24},$ and we have that 

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\frac{0.24}{n}}.
$$

We require that the standard error is less than $0.01\,\text{ft}.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{0.24}{n}} & <0.01 \\ \sqrt{n} & >\frac{\sqrt{0.24}}{0.01} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{\frac{0.24}{{0.01}^{2}}} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{2\,400} \\ n & >2\,400.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest sample size is $n=2\,401.$"} {:db/id 17592186447168 :question/id #uuid "74bfeec3-3f4e-5c4f-b7e4-18502ff50810" :question/math-academy-id "q-143443" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "52aca894-e775-54c1-8b43-216acbc28ba1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "50" :db/id 17592186447162} {:answer/id #uuid "99113dff-3b5a-5c2f-a393-160c589b1310" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "201" :db/id 17592186447163} {:answer/id #uuid "bc3f329b-2d56-5c65-8fd5-ce307d766978" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186447164} {:answer/id #uuid "c6919965-008c-583a-804a-02b29893ad0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "401" :db/id 17592186447165} {:answer/id #uuid "f7eb1986-1eeb-5a7e-94d4-f2aae2d2a16c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "901" :db/id 17592186447166}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186447165} :answer-field/id #uuid "962adc96-285b-55db-b3b2-45bc705d2628" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186447167}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ drawn from a population with mean $\mu =100$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=25,$  determine the smallest sample size required so that the standard error of the mean is less than $0.25.$" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

drawn from a population with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2,$ then the sample mean, denoted $\overline{X},$ is given by

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
$$

The sample mean is a random variable whose probability distribution (also called the **sampling distribution**) has an expected value of $\mu\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu
$$

 

In other words, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean $\mu.$

Let's now find the variance of the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}.$ Using the properties of variance for sums of independent random variables, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}] & =\text{Var}[\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}] \\  & ={(\frac{1}{n})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \text{Var}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot (\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+⋯+\text{Var}[{X}_{n}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot ({\sigma }^{2}+{\sigma }^{2}+⋯+{\sigma }^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot n{\sigma }^{2} \\  & =\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, we have the following important result:

$$
\textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}
$$

It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}.$ What we *do* know is that whatever the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}$ is, it has mean $\mu$ and variance $$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the nails in the population have lengths $5\,\text{cm}$ and $\text{10}\,\text{cm},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $4:1.$ Therefore, to compute the population mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $4+1=5$ nails only with the following lengths:

$$
5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm}\,10\,\text{cm}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot 5+10) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(20+10) \\  & =\frac{30}{5} \\  & =6\,\text{cm},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot {5}^{2}+{10}^{2})-{6}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(200)-36 \\  & =40-36 \\  & =4\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sample size $n=3,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}=\frac{4}{3}\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}≈1.15\,\text{cm}
$$

$$

We're told that the employees in the population have working hours $38\,\text{h/week}$ and $40\,\text{h/week},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $3:1.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $3+1=4$ employees only with the following working hours:

$$

$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{4}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(3\cdot 38+40) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(114+40) \\  & =\frac{154}{4} \\  & =38.5\,\text{h/week},\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(3\cdot {38}^{2}+{40}^{2})-{38.5}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(5\,932)-1\,482.25 \\  & =1\,483-1\,482.25 \\  & =0.75\,{(\text{h/week})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the population standard deviation is $\sigma =\sqrt{0.75},$ and we have that 

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{n}} & <0.5 \\ \sqrt{n} & >\frac{\sqrt{0.75}}{0.5} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{{0.5}^{2}}} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{0.25}} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{3} \\ n & >3.\end{aligned}
$$

biologist is experimenting with bacteria stored in a Petri dish. She observes that the number of bacteria in the dish *triples* every hour. If there were $100$ bacteria initially, can she determine how many bacteria will be present after $3$ hours?

Starting with $100$ bacteria, she knows that this number *triples* after one hour. Remember that tripling means to multiply by a factor of $3$.

To get the number of bacteria after one hour, we multiply the initial amount by $3$:

$$
\color{blue}{100\cdot 3}
$$

After another hour ($2$ hours in total), the number above triples again. So to get the total number of bacteria after $2$ hours, we multiply the amount above by $3$:

$$
({\color{blue}{100\cdot 3}})\cdot 3 = {\color{red}{100 \cdot 3^2}}
$$

And after another hour ($3$ hours total), the number above triples once again:

$$
({\color{red}{100 \cdot 3^2}})\cdot 3 = 100 \cdot 3^3
$$

If we evaluate the above expression, we get

$$
100 \cdot 3^3 = 100\cdot 27 = 2\,700
$$

So after $3$ hours, there will be $2\,700$ bacteria in the Petri dish.

This is an example of **exponential growth**. The number of bacteria triples over a time interval of $1$ hour, every hour. The total number of bacteria grows very rapidly, as we can see from the chart below.

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 2 \leq \sqrt{xy} \leq 4, \: 2x \leq y \leq 3x \big\}
$$

and the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where $u=\dfrac{y}{x}$ and $v=xy.$ Find the representation of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}(D)$ in the $uv$-plane." :question/worked-solution "Notice that $\mathbf{T}^{-1}(D)$ is the image of $D$ under the action of the transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Let's find the image of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}(D)$ in the $uv$-plane. To do that, we write the region $D$ in terms of $u$ and $v,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(D) & ={(u,v)\,:\,2\le \sqrt{xy}\le 4,\,2x\le y\le 3x} \\  & ={(u,v)\,:\,{2}^{2}\le (\sqrt{xy})^{2}\le {4}^{2},\,2\le \frac{y}{x}\le 3} \\  & ={(u,v)\,:\,4\le xy\le 16,\,2\le \frac{y}{x}\le 3} \\  & ={(u,v)\,:\,4\le v\le 16,\,2\le u\le 3} \\  & ={(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 3,\,4\le v\le 16}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $2 \leq \sqrt{xy}\leq 4,$ we must have $x \neq 0.$ Therefore, $u=\dfrac{y}{x}$ is well-defined."} {:db/id 17592186049373} {:db/id 17592186198949 :question/id #uuid "9156e571-2fe9-5347-95da-c1c97de1a3c9" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Transformation That Maps a Region Onto a Type I Region"}] :question/problem "Let $D$ be the finite region bounded by the curve 
$(x+y)^2 + y = 3$ and the line $y=-1.$
Consider the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where $u=x+y$ and $v=y.$ Find the representation of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}(D)$ in the $uv$-plane." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we are given that  

![](images/61/61a3c6677ac0c20f5cccc6808fa7b078f91c3ad784d59167d11a9829cd0f86c3.png)

Substituting $x+y = u$ and $y = v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{2}+y=3\,⟹\,{u}^{2}+v=3\,⟹\,v=3-{u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y = v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=-1\,⟹\,v=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v=3-{u}^{2} \\ v=-1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm 2 \\ v=-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2, -1).$

![](images/84/84c624aab456b9a090c9c4e6d23c82d8e1f69425050b6f3ee9d4afd18e3f0cec.png)

As a result, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation 

$$
\mathbf{T}^{-1}(D)  = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -2 \leq u \leq 2, \quad  -1 \leq v \leq 3-u^2 \big\}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050822} {:db/id 17592186050984} {:db/id 17592186199004 :question/id #uuid "d20a7000-9bdd-5db4-9bc9-aa97236edf93" :question/math-academy-id "q-82669"} {:db/id 17592186199006 Substituting $x+{y}^{3}=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+{y}^{3})^{2}-y=1\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=1\,⟹\,v={u}^{2}-1,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2\,⟹\,v=2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2}-1 \\ v=2\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm \sqrt{3} \\ v=2.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt{3},2).$

![](images/fc/fc6e896f50255deea574c52014935097b6c0b49aa6a1e54a9d6a484dc1b8cc61.png)

As a result, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation 

$$
{T}^{-1}(D)={(u,v)\,:\,-\sqrt{3}\le u\le \sqrt{3},\,{u}^{2}-1\le v\le 2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186371471 :question/id #uuid "1b873e65-1368-56e9-97b4-a7ec190bdcf6" :question/math-academy-id "q-103969"} {:db/id 17592186373298 :question/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Let $D$ be the finite region bounded by the curve 
$(x-y)^{2}+x+y=0$ and  the line $y=0.$ 
Consider the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where $u=x-y$ and $v=x+y.$ Find the representation of ${T}^{-1}(D)$ in the $uv$-plane." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we are given that 

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x-y \\ x+y\end{aligned}].
$$

Substituting $x-y=u$ and $x+y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-y)^{2}+x+y=0\,⟹\,(x-y)^{2}+(x+y)=0\,⟹\,v=-{u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Now, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}x-y=u \\ x+y=v\end{aligned}\,⟹\,y=\frac{v-u}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this value into the equation of the given line yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\, & ⟹\,\frac{v-u}{2}=0 & \,⟹\,v=u\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, to find the intersections of the resulting lines in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v=-{u}^{2} \\ v=u\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u(u+1)=0 \\ v=u.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(-1,-1).$ 

![](images/05/05d7e65dca3c6d116d01be9e57fc83f3e3edcda4135a3f96fea82af8db4f2d1e.png)

As a result, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation 

$$
{T}^{-1}(D)={(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 0,\,u\le v\le -{u}^{2}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198376 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198018 :question/id #uuid "87c2cf96-8772-5b28-b6d8-a5616b38543f" :question/math-academy-id "e-12337"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "de3fa2fa-304c-583a-8c73-a5ff1db972e2" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198556 :question/id #uuid "a658a37a-3d38-50b3-a715-a52c9415984e" :question/math-academy-id "q-123917"} {:db/id 17592186198582 :question/id #uuid "f0c60c12-3acb-5c5a-8aba-c02d0db96c2a" :question/math-academy-id "q-160559"} {:db/id 17592186371920 :question/id #uuid "ec93a22b-8046-55ff-bd79-1effdf7c3586" :question/math-academy-id "q-161075"} {:db/id 17592186371927 :question/id #uuid "d859aec4-6186-5f7b-b172-35e5234e06b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-161084"} {:db/id 17592186371934 :question/id #uuid "21e23291-6559-5eea-9b70-7fd00996880f" :question/math-academy-id "q-161085"} {:db/id 17592186398500 :question/id #uuid "e82a0cbf-06e5-5031-a4c7-160ebc24fbd2" :question/math-academy-id "q-161086"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Transformation That Maps a Rectangular Region Onto a Given One"} {:db/id 17592186198018 :question/id #uuid "87c2cf96-8772-5b28-b6d8-a5616b38543f" :question/math-academy-id "e-12337" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186198376 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "de3fa2fa-304c-583a-8c73-a5ff1db972e2" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Transformation That Maps a Rectangular Region Onto a Given One"}] :question/problem "Consider the finite region $D$ enclosed in the first quadrant of the $xy$-plane between the curves

$$
y=x, \qquad
y=7x, \qquad
x=\dfrac{3}{y^2}, \qquad
x=\dfrac{5}{y^2}.
$$

A transformation $\mathbf{T},$ where

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

maps a rectangular region $\Delta$ with sides parallel to the $u$- and $v$-axes from the $uv$-plane onto $D$ in the $xy$-plane. Given that

$$
\mathbf{T} : (u,v) \to \Big(\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{v}{u^2}}, \: \bbox[5pt, white, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}} \, \Big),
$$

what could be the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "We would like to find a rectangular region of the form

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v)\,:\,a\le u\le b,\,\,c\le v\le d} \\  & ={(u,v)\,:\,a\le u(x,y)\le b,\,\,c\le v(x,y)\le d},\end{aligned}
$$

where the equations of the left, right, bottom, and top sides are

$$
{\color{blue}u(x,y)} = a, \qquad 
{\color{blue}u(x,y)} = b, \qquad
{\color{red}v(x,y)} = c, \qquad 
{\color{red}v(x,y)} = d.
$$

With that in mind, let's analyze the boundary of our region $D.$ 

Rewriting the equations 

$$
y=x, \qquad
y=7x, \qquad
x=\dfrac{3}{y^2}, \qquad
x=\dfrac{5}{y^2}
$$

by moving both variables $x$ and $y$ to the left-hand side, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x}=1,\,\frac{y}{x}=7,\,x{y}^{2}=3,\,x{y}^{2}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we put $u(x,y)={\color{blue}\dfrac{y}{x}}$ and $v(x,y)={\color{red}xy^2},$ we can define the transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ as

$$
\mathbf{T}^{-1} : (x,y) \to \left( \, {\color{blue}\dfrac{y}{x}}\,, \: \bbox[2pt, white, border: 1pt solid black]{\color{red}xy^2} \right).
$$

To find $\mathbf{T},$ we should express $x$ and $y$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$ Recall that we have

$$
{\begin{aligned}u=\frac{y}{x} \\ v=x{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, $y=ux.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get 

$$
v = u^2x^3
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x^3 = \dfrac{v}{u^2} 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{v}{u^2}}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{v}{u^2}}$ back into $y=ux,$ we obtain

$$
y =u\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{v}{u^2}} = \sqrt[3]{uv}.
$$

Therefore, the transformation $\mathbf{T}$ can be given by

$$
\mathbf{T} : (u,v) \to \left(\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{v}{u^2}}, \, \bbox[2pt, white, border: 1pt solid black]{ \sqrt[3]{uv}} \right).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198556 :question/id #uuid "a658a37a-3d38-50b3-a715-a52c9415984e" :question/math-academy-id "q-123917"} {:db/id 17592186198582 :question/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186199252 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199452 :tutorial/content "The plane region $D$ shown below is defined as

$$D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq xe^{y}\leq 4, \: \: 1 \leq x^2e^{-2y} \leq 3 \big\}.$$

![](images/17/17e133a50f4a587a26fbf0914c1dc08106ecb822e1e88ba5e7280a10215221c0.png)

This region is pretty complicated, which could make it difficult to work with.

So, we'd like to define a transformation

$$\mathbf T^{-1}: (x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$$ that maps the region $D$ to a rectangular region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane.

![](images/d2/d26df05b3200a01f2b6fba5a1c04e8d178c88f40e078309c71329bcdfcc91ac2.png)

How can we find such a transformation?

Looking at the bounding curves that make up the structure of $D,$ we consider the transformation

$${\color{red}u}={\color{red}{xe^{y}}}, \qquad {\color{blue}v}={\color{blue}{x^2e^{-2y}}}.$$

Next, we find our expression for $\Delta$ by writing $D$ in terms of $u$ and $v,$ as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}Δ={T}^{-1}(D) & ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le x{e}^{y}\le 4,\,\,1\le {x}^{2}{e}^{-2y}\le 3} \\ & ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,\,1\le v\le 3}\end{aligned}$$

And that's all there is to it! We've successfully found a transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ that maps the complicated region $D$ in the $xy$-plane to the rectangle $[1,4]\times[1,3]$ in the $uv$-plane.

![](images/64/6423e8d59e07acda3c8d84e47852ad95f37d9fdf39c3669a8227c224a0cbb54a.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f2467b8-6aa5-598d-bd70-646d2f6c5588" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4410 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "81de6675-7ea1-553a-9697-f6798481631b" :step/math-academy-id 27105 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199253}} {:db/id 17592186199253 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198362 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198236 :question/id #uuid "6d2cd5bf-899f-5b81-9512-ee98489d17ac" :question/math-academy-id "e-7322"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a6d98056-016e-520b-b752-d6a529f2c02d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049373}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198949} {:db/id 17592186199005} {:db/id 17592186371443} {:db/id 17592186371450}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Rectangular Preimage Given a Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "a16a89f0-4b6c-571e-8667-09aa727ed945" :step/math-academy-id 27106 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199276}} {:db/id 17592186199254 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198363 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198237 :question/id #uuid "c78f087b-f0e5-58e6-a7a1-92a78c85c4d9" :question/math-academy-id "e-7323"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9156e571-2fe9-5347-95da-c1c97de1a3c9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050822} {:db/id 17592186050984}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186199004} {:db/id 17592186199006} {:db/id 17592186371457} {:db/id 17592186371464} {:db/id 17592186371471} {:db/id 17592186373298} {:db/id 17592186373374}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Transformation That Maps a Region Onto a Type I Region"} :step/id #uuid "548a6670-5a09-5138-83d9-a4ddc9f4a9dc" :step/math-academy-id 27107} {:db/id 17592186199255 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199453 :tutorial/content "We often use transformations to map a region in the $xy$-plane to a type I region in the $uv$-plane.

For example, let $D$ be the region bounded by the curve $(x+y)^2 - y = 2$ and the line $y=1,$ as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/d7/d7df2aa53d64cbd13c784a6dc5d827027f56cc8e63917bbd9a324f7576f3dfa6.png)

This is not a type I region because the lower curve is not an explicit function of $x.$

Let's map $D$ to a type I region in the $uv$-plane. First, let $\mathbf T$ be the transformation

$$\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$$

The equations of the bounding curves suggest the following for the transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

$${\color{blue}{u}}={\color{blue}{x+y}}, \qquad {\color{red}{v}}={\color{red}{y}}.$$

Substituting ${\color{blue}{u}}={\color{blue}{x+y}}$ and ${\color{red}{v}}={\color{red}{y}}$ into the equation of the lower curve, we get

$$\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{2}-y=2\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=2\,⟹\,v={u}^{2}-2,\end{aligned}$$ which is the equation of an upward-opening parabola.

Substituting $y = v$ into the equation of the line, we obtain

$$\begin{aligned}y=1\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}$$

To find the intersections of the parabola and line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2}-2 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm \sqrt{3} \\ v=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt3, 1).$

![](images/5b/5b52258abe08675938210de54c53dafe474e753249341c36833b8286259144ee.png)

Finally, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the following type I representation: $$\mathbf{T}^{-1}(D) = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -\sqrt3 \leq u \leq \sqrt3, \quad u^2-2 \leq v \leq 1 \big\}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6de07339-5bd1-5441-867a-164b51b62c5e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4411 :tutorial/title "Transformations That Map a Region to a Type I Region"} :step/id #uuid "708c40ea-21c0-5791-80ec-1f7934311a44" :step/math-academy-id 27113 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199254}} {:db/id 17592186199276 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198376 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198018 :question/id #uuid "87c2cf96-8772-5b28-b6d8-a5616b38543f" :question/math-academy-id "e-12337"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "de3fa2fa-304c-583a-8c73-a5ff1db972e2" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198556} {:db/id 17592186198582} {:db/id 17592186371920} {:db/id 17592186371927} {:db/id 17592186371934} {:db/id 17592186398500}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Transformation That Maps a Rectangular Region Onto a Given One"} :step/id #uuid "b3d2c730-410c-5244-b2a9-29f37c6ec44b" :step/math-academy-id 44206 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199255}}] :activity/title "Transformations of Regions Between Curves" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198480} {:db/id 17592186199252 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199452 :tutorial/content "The plane region $D$ shown below is defined as

:step/content {:db/id 17592186199453 :tutorial/content "We often use transformations to map a region in the $xy$-plane to a type I region in the $uv$-plane.

For example, let $D$ be the region bounded by the curve $(x+y)^2 - y = 2$ and the line $y=1,$ as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/d7/d7df2aa53d64cbd13c784a6dc5d827027f56cc8e63917bbd9a324f7576f3dfa6.png)

This is not a type I region because the lower curve is not an explicit function of $x.$

Let's map $D$ to a type I region in the $uv$-plane. First, let $\mathbf T$ be the transformation

$$\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$$

The equations of the bounding curves suggest the following for the transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

$${\color{blue}{u}}={\color{blue}{x+y}}, \qquad {\color{red}{v}}={\color{red}{y}}.$$

Substituting ${\color{blue}{u}}={\color{blue}{x+y}}$ and ${\color{red}{v}}={\color{red}{y}}$ into the equation of the lower curve, we get

$$\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{2}-y=2\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=2\,⟹\,v={u}^{2}-2,\end{aligned}$$ which is the equation of an upward-opening parabola.

Substituting $y = v$ into the equation of the line, we obtain

$$\begin{aligned}y=1\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}$$

To find the intersections of the parabola and line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2}-2 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm \sqrt{3} \\ v=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt3, 1).$

![](images/5b/5b52258abe08675938210de54c53dafe474e753249341c36833b8286259144ee.png)

Finally, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the following type I representation: $$\mathbf{T}^{-1}(D) = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -\sqrt3 \leq u \leq \sqrt3, \quad u^2-2 \leq v \leq 1 \big\}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6de07339-5bd1-5441-867a-164b51b62c5e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4411 :tutorial/title "Transformations That Map a Region to a Type I Region"} :step/id #uuid "708c40ea-21c0-5791-80ec-1f7934311a44" :step/math-academy-id 27113 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199254}} {:db/id 17592186199453 :tutorial/content "We often use transformations to map a region in the $xy$-plane to a type I region in the $uv$-plane.

Let's map $D$ to a type I region in the $uv$-plane. First, let $\mathbf T$ be the transformation

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the matrices given below. Find $\text{dim(Null}(A))+\text{dim(Null}(B))+\text{dim(Null}(C)).$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -4 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -7 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "The dimension of the null space of a matrix is the number of non-pivot columns in the matrix. 

Also, all of the given matrices are in row echelon form.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the statements.

- The matrix $A$ has $2$ pivot columns and $1$ non-pivot column (namely, the $2$nd column). So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(A))=1.
$$

- The matrix $B$ has $2$ pivot columns and $2$ non-pivot columns (namely, the $2$nd and $4$th columns). So, 

$$

:question/worked-solution "Recall that by definition, $\text{nullity}(D)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(D)).$

To find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(D))$, we reduce $D$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 5 & -7 & 9 \\ -3 & 6 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ -3 & 6 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix has $3$ pivot columns and no non-pivot columns. 

Therefore,

$$

$$

The reduced matrix has $3$ pivot columns and no non-pivot columns. 

Therefore,

$$
\text{nullity}(A)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A))=0.

$\textrm{dim(Null}(A))$ is equal to the number of *non-pivot* columns in the corresponding row echelon form of $A$

:db/id 17592186320450}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "da3efbc4-2fa4-54a8-9aa9-e1c2c723490a" :question/math-academy-id "q-35316" :question/problem "Consider the matrices given below. Find $\,\text{dim(Null}(A))+\text{dim(Null}(B))+\text{dim(Null}(C)).$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 7 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "The dimension of the null space of a matrix is the number of non-pivot columns in the matrix. 

Also, all of the given matrices are in row echelon form.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the statements.

- The matrix $A$ has $3$ pivot columns and no non-pivot column. So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(A))=0.
$$

- The matrix $B$ has $1$ pivot column and $1$ non-pivot column (namely, the $2$nd column). So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(B))=1.
$$

- The matrix $C$ has $3$ pivot columns and $1$ non-pivot column (namely, the $4$th column). So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(C))=1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\text{dim(Null}(A))+\text{dim(Null}(B))+\text{dim(Null}(C))=0+1+1=2.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "034d01d2-7fd8-5b65-910e-ac88f27f255e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436687}} {:db/id 17592186436687 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124876 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28e68488-3044-5580-9e3c-089a9a1d218e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186319521} {:answer/id #uuid "35be0dfc-5948-5bd3-9dac-1c20570872cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186319559} {:answer/id #uuid "5502e90e-05b0-5dfe-b4f5-71b52399a4d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186319638} {:answer/id #uuid "961f532b-51e7-5809-ad29-5c12359cfab4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186319833} {:answer/id #uuid "ec49169a-3f2a-5743-b17d-b75c92825009" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186320098}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186319833} :answer-field/id #uuid "2a5d0bf9-0555-588a-8937-9468b4e30755" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186320257}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6a0b3d6d-593b-5e4e-ba8b-3eae5b6b11d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-35345" :question/problem "If $D=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 5 & -7 & 9 \\ -3 & 6 & -1\end{aligned}],\,$ then $\text{nullity}(D)=$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that by definition, $\text{nullity}(D)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(D)).$

To find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(D))$, we reduce $D$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 5 & -7 & 9 \\ -3 & 6 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ -3 & 6 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix has $3$ pivot columns and no non-pivot columns. 

Therefore,

$$
\text{nullity}(D)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(D))=0.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4760dd1d-3298-58a3-b976-41ff6b4b2fae" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436689}} {:db/id 17592186436688 :step/content {:db/id 17592186436685 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "11bd5b8c-479c-5cc6-b6bf-6871d03b08d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186436673} {:answer/id #uuid "5cb2151a-b33e-521e-b8b0-24402371cbfb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186436675} {:answer/id #uuid "7de2f3de-7c9b-5a4b-bf43-493cdbc1ac7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186436676} {:answer/id #uuid "b84ac634-ebd3-56af-8b44-0c0dd0d7b70e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186436677} {:answer/id #uuid "c9a9fef4-70fb-5285-b43b-261546c9e8bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186436679}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186436673} :answer-field/id #uuid "a4adc5e4-eeb4-5d02-8d02-ca9f53944067" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186436682}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e39062c0-8f9b-52cc-adaa-1df745d5f896" :question/math-academy-id "q-79346" :question/problem "Consider the matrices given below. $$" :question/worked-solution "The dimension of the null space of a matrix is the number of non-pivot columns in the matrix. 

Also, all of the given matrices are in row echelon form.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the statements.

$$

- The matrix $B$ has $1$ pivot column and $1$ non-pivot columns. So, 

$$

$$

- The matrix $C$ has $2$ pivot columns and $2$ non-pivot columns (namely, the $2$nd and the $4$th columns). So, 

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$" :question/worked-solution "The dimension of the null space of a matrix is the number of non-pivot columns in the matrix. 

Also, all of the given matrices are in row echelon form.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the statements.

- The matrix $A$ has $2$ pivot columns and $1$ non-pivot column (namely, the $2$nd column). So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(A))=1.
$$

- The matrix $B$ has $1$ pivot column and $1$ non-pivot columns. So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(B))=1.
$$

- The matrix $C$ has $2$ pivot columns and $2$ non-pivot columns (namely, the $2$nd and the $4$th columns). So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(C))=2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\text{dim(Null}(A))+\text{dim(Null}(B))+\text{dim(Null}(C))=1+1+2=4.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5674bd5f-5ced-5ae8-83dc-206575be79e5"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "11bd5b8c-479c-5cc6-b6bf-6871d03b08d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" What is the equation of the ellipse given above?" :question/worked-solution "Remember that the general equation of an ellipse centered at $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the ellipse is centered at $(-4,0),$ the horizontal radius has length $a=2,$ and the vertical radius has length $b=6.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-(-4))^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{(y-0)^{2}}{{6}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+4)^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{36} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186284555 :question/id #uuid "6910717e-3c06-5400-8f4a-4be89ee6a847" :question/math-academy-id "q-16553"} {:db/id 17592186294963 :question/id #uuid "769c3ba1-be44-5d72-ab21-003c024cdeed" :question/math-academy-id "q-278251" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186087833 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "57e19ee3-db9a-58d7-8ca3-4e8801aee656" :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Equation of a Tall Ellipse"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f9e4e68f-490a-50ec-831b-a2606c9e2e81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{16}" :db/id 17592186293914}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "f9e4e68f-490a-50ec-831b-a2606c9e2e81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{16}" :db/id 17592186293914} :answer-field/id #uuid "a6cc6684-109c-5446-8ce1-df88d1548753" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186294528}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "![](images/6b/6bb7a8dc9b34c03e5456b84b843c8975aac8ec8f09135fe9069693febc24ba78.png)

\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.

$$

$$

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?" :question/worked-solution "Remember that the general equation of an ellipse centered at $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the ellipse is centered at $(-1,-1),$ the horizontal radius has length $a=1,$ and the vertical radius has length $b=2.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

If a pump can empty $\dfrac{3}{2}$ of a pool in $15$ minutes, then how many minutes will it take the pump to empty all $5$ pools?" :question/worked-solution "To find the number of minutes that the pump takes to empty $5$ pools, we can first find the unit rate of minutes per pool, and then multiply the unit rate by $5$ pools.

To find the unit rate of minutes per pool, we divide the number of minutes, $15$, by the number of pools,

$$
\dfrac{3}{2}
$$

as follows:

$$
15 \div \dfrac{3}{2}
$$

To divide by a fraction, we multiply by the fraction's reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}
15 \div \frac{3}{2} &= 15 \cdot \frac{2}{3} \\
&= \frac{15}{1} \cdot \frac{2}{3} \\
&= \frac{15 \cdot 2}{1 \cdot 3} \\
&= \frac{30}{3} \\
&= 30 \div 3 \\
&= 10
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the unit rate is $10$ minutes per pool. To find the number of minutes that the pump takes to empty $5$ pools, we multiply the unit rate by $5$ pools and get

$$
\begin{aligned}
10 \cdot 5 &= 50
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the pump will take $50$ minutes to empty $5$ pools."} {:db/id 17592186049357} {:db/id 17592186074496 :question/id #uuid "90a082f1-f01b-5405-832a-52195f52162d" :question/math-academy-id "q-68635"} {:db/id 17592186074505 :question/id #uuid "d0472b8f-8f4d-5e82-89f9-e04746b79227" :question/math-academy-id "q-69020"} {:db/id 17592186073726 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073637 :question/id #uuid "4f61ec9c-9b87-5b25-9543-44b6043b7b4a" :question/math-academy-id "e-4747"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d34e60c9-710b-50ca-a491-adc2b50e6edc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049616}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074495 :question/id #uuid "a7588b8e-0546-5d04-bcb6-9db67ed6acb0" :question/math-academy-id "q-68631"} {:db/id 17592186074506 :question/id #uuid "0cd685c4-4752-5924-b3d5-4f3981ddea7a" :question/math-academy-id "q-69038"}] :knowledge-point/title "Problem Solving Using the Ratio of Two Fractions"} {:db/id 17592186073637 :question/id #uuid "4f61ec9c-9b87-5b25-9543-44b6043b7b4a" :question/math-academy-id "e-4747" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186073726 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d34e60c9-710b-50ca-a491-adc2b50e6edc" :knowledge-point/title "Problem Solving Using the Ratio of Two Fractions"}] :question/problem "Ava works in a coffee store. How much of a bonus will Ava earn if she sells $18$ liters of coffee?" :question/worked-solution "To find the number of dollars that Ava earns if she sells $18$ liters of coffee, we can first find the unit rate of dollars per liter, and then multiply the unit rate by $18$ liters.

To find the unit rate of dollars per liter, we divide the number of dollars,

$$
\dfrac{3}{4}
$$

by the number of liters,

$$
\dfrac{3}{8}
$$

as follows:

$$
\dfrac{3}{4} \div \dfrac{3}{8}
$$

Dividing one fraction by another is equivalent to multiplying the fraction by the reciprocal of the second fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{3}{4} \div \frac{3}{8} &= \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{8}{3} \\
&= \frac{3 \cdot 8}{4 \cdot 3} \\
&= \frac{24}{12} \\
&= 24 \div 12 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the unit rate is $2$ dollars per liter. To find the number of dollars that Ava earns selling $18$ liters, we multiply the unit rate by $18$ liters and get

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 \cdot 18 &= 36
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, Ava earns $36$ dollars if she sells $18$ liters of coffee."} {:db/id 17592186049616} {:db/id 17592186074495 :question/id #uuid "a7588b8e-0546-5d04-bcb6-9db67ed6acb0" Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\text{Ker}(T)={0}$
- **II.** $\text{rank}(T)=4$
- **III.** $T(v)=0$ for some $v\ne 0$" :question/worked-solution "Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{4}$ into ${R}^{4},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{4} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=4 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Since $T$ is a bijection, the invertible matrix theorem implies that $\text{Ker}(T)={0}.$

- Statement II is true. Since $T$ is a bijection, the invertible matrix theorem implies that $\text{rank}(T)=4.$

- Statement III is false. Since $T$ is a bijection, the invertible matrix theorem implies that $\text{Ker}(T)={0},$ which means there is no non-zero vector $v$ such that $T(v)=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} {:db/id 17592186326727 :question/id #uuid "8e6f3463-c123-5a14-aa68-90e5211244ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-38905"} {:db/id 17592186326728 - Statement II is true. Since $T$ is not invertible, the invertible matrix theorem implies that  $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement III is false. Since $T$ is not invertible, the invertible matrix theorem implies that $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0.$

We have the following theorem regarding invertible linear transformations: 

*If ![](images/c1/c15eeb9e7a3ff525fbdcd2f175622bd034f0b34899224f9ce2e08a5300d625de.svg) is the standard matrix of ![](images/ee/eefe57a16ee4b7baeb91597e3e1f25ed4fa583bffef387058ee3d4c563ae7809.svg), then ![](images/ee/eefe57a16ee4b7baeb91597e3e1f25ed4fa583bffef387058ee3d4c563ae7809.svg) is invertible if and only if ![](images/c1/c15eeb9e7a3ff525fbdcd2f175622bd034f0b34899224f9ce2e08a5300d625de.svg) is invertible*.

Recall that the invertible matrix theorem in terms of dimension, rank, and nullity states that if ![](images/c1/c15eeb9e7a3ff525fbdcd2f175622bd034f0b34899224f9ce2e08a5300d625de.svg) is an ![](images/3e/3e214695b86d4170ea46f8cd0f8a4fd78e3d1c3a6abab1e8de1e3c35634c10a1.svg) matrix, then

![](images/28/281f907860a395891d590680f527a1eee8be046879da8f3607669a22cae5e5d2.svg)

In the theorem above, we can make the following swaps, where ![](images/ee/eefe57a16ee4b7baeb91597e3e1f25ed4fa583bffef387058ee3d4c563ae7809.svg) is a linear transformation with the standard matrix ![](images/70/70836ef8c789fb64a4b4a4b29a48074c146b8374116c1eeca4e3251def9e7d80.svg)
![](images/96/9607abc75a2c67c4a11635cb9c84d6f575582d9961a822bdbf3d5e056536a9ce.svg)

:question/math-academy-id "q-84053" :question/problem "Let $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T$ and ${u}_{1},{u}_{2}\in {R}^{3}.$  Consider the following statement:

*If ${u}_{1}-{u}_{2}\ne 0$ and $T({u}_{1})-T({u}_{2})=0,$ then $\text{__________}.$*

Which of the following can be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?
- **I.** $\text{Ker}(T)={0}$
- **II.** $\text{rank}(T)\ne 3$
- **III.** $T$ is invertible

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since $T$ is a linear transformation and $T({u}_{1})-T({u}_{2})=0,$ we have $T({u}_{1}-{u}_{2})=0.$ So ${u}_{1}-{u}_{2}\in \text{Ker}(T)$ and ${u}_{1}-{u}_{2}\ne 0.$ Therefore, we must have $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement II is true. Since $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}$, then $\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)\ne 3.$

- Statement III is false. According to the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{rank}(T)\ne 3,$ the transformation $T$ can't be invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} :step/id #uuid "291db6d3-4728-529e-a9be-f15ca20db25d"} {:db/id 17592186417706 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125164 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "da97a065-c9ea-545d-9832-58ba5595c282" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186460017} {:answer/id #uuid "44b485c0-4b9e-522d-95c5-7ceba53f1f39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186460018}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186460017} :answer-field/id #uuid "efff0b18-702b-56a0-8bdf-765f60a773b3" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186460875} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "74ec198b-aef3-59b6-b091-30d662e9f4cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186460019} {:answer/id #uuid "a7f8d74d-cce4-5aab-b18a-c61877075bdb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186460020}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186460020} :answer-field/id #uuid "9908404e-2262-51c4-b8db-2672114ba2d0" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186460876} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a0734130-7b87-5408-bf8e-b097433b8280" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186460021} {:answer/id #uuid "b49d1b8e-67c2-5af5-8d46-21f059350ab6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186460022}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186460021} :answer-field/id #uuid "6141e94f-e3cc-500f-ba91-1f18aa4e01ca" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186460877}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "a059dc0b-5296-5e25-93e6-3ffd38125f6c" :question/math-academy-id "q-47556" :question/problem "Let $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T.$ Consider the following statement:

The line shown above passes through the points $(0,-2)$ and $(2,2)$." :question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form

$$
y=mx+b
$$

So, we need to work out the slope $m$ and the $y$-intercept $b$.

From the graph, we see that the line intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,-2)$. So, the $y$-intercept is $b = -2$.

We can calculate the slope of the line by choosing two points on the line and applying the slope formula. The line passes through the points $(0,-2)$ and $(2,2)$, so we calculate its slope as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m &= \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}} \\
&= (2 - (-2))/(2 - 0) \\
&= \frac{4}{2} \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the slope $m = 2$ and the $y$-intercept $b = -2$ into the slope-intercept form

$$
y = mx + b
$$

we obtain the equation of the line:
$y = 2x - 2$."} {:db/id 17592186101258 :question/id #uuid "78b15dc1-cbef-5898-ab15-04cac6cf3f71" :question/math-academy-id "q-178577"} {:db/id 17592186101322 :question/id #uuid "6a759b29-8959-5d61-bf0a-e37d1c25750b" :question/math-academy-id "q-22321"} {:db/id 17592186101323 :question/id #uuid "53faa267-d958-560f-8a88-e6fda6aff20c" :question/math-academy-id "q-22322"} {:db/id 17592186101009 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100617 :question/id #uuid "206b8f86-4184-50fa-9999-08700d10dc4f" :question/math-academy-id "e-20867"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8ac060cb-0c76-5050-9156-e5f17ad26fbb" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101324 :question/id #uuid "cd5123ca-c223-5418-9397-60db6f948f70" :question/math-academy-id "q-22606"} {:db/id 17592186101521 :question/id #uuid "20f8d459-b120-51d4-bc86-2e2f178cb14d" :question/math-academy-id "q-6899"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Equation of a Graphed Line (Negative Slope)"} {:db/id 17592186100617 :question/id #uuid "206b8f86-4184-50fa-9999-08700d10dc4f" :question/math-academy-id "e-20867" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186101009 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8ac060cb-0c76-5050-9156-e5f17ad26fbb" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Equation of a Graphed Line (Negative Slope)"}] :question/problem "Find the equation of the line shown below.

![](images/42/4298ec9c12555fd5e87265617ee274ef0fa859decd3ccd9473dfe8f778492df0.png)" :question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form

$$
y=mx+b
$$

So, we need to work out the slope $m$ and the $y$-intercept $b$.

From the graph, we see that the line intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,2)$. So, the $y$-intercept is $b=2$.

We can calculate the slope of the line by choosing two points on the line and applying the slope formula. The line passes through the points $(0,2)$ and $(6,0)$, so we calculate its slope as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m &= \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}} \\
&= \frac{0 - 2}{6 - 0} \\
&= \frac{-2}{6} \\
&=-\frac{1}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the slope

$$
m=-\dfrac{1}{3}
$$

and the $y$-intercept $b=2$ into the slope-intercept form

$$
y=mx+b
$$

we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
y=-\dfrac{1}{3}x+2
$$"} {:db/id 17592186101324 :question/id #uuid "cd5123ca-c223-5418-9397-60db6f948f70" :question/math-academy-id "q-22606"} {:db/id 17592186101521 :question/id #uuid "20f8d459-b120-51d4-bc86-2e2f178cb14d" :question/math-academy-id "q-6899"} {:db/id 17592186101010 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100595 :question/id #uuid "8351e1cb-c602-5968-be5a-9c337ad977de" :question/math-academy-id "e-12853"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4762cb71-f6b6-5d32-8d0b-a457db66ff97" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101260 :question/id #uuid "c0b425fb-b8a2-5723-acb7-016f2e613ac7" :question/math-academy-id "q-179507"} {:db/id 17592186101522 :question/id #uuid "51cb6080-077c-56de-a53e-403e56ffa583" :question/math-academy-id "q-6900"} {:db/id 17592186101523 :question/id #uuid "0931729f-a266-5a5d-8a3c-2f6e56e97d48" :question/math-academy-id "q-6947"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Equation of a Line That Passes Through Two Points: Y-Intercept Given"} {:db/id 17592186100595 :question/id #uuid "8351e1cb-c602-5968-be5a-9c337ad977de" :question/math-academy-id "e-12853" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186101010 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4762cb71-f6b6-5d32-8d0b-a457db66ff97" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Equation of a Line That Passes Through Two Points: Y-Intercept Given"}] :question/problem "Calculate the equation of the straight line that passes through the points $(0,8)$ and $(3,2)$." :question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form

:topic/math-academy-id 330} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065281 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065416 :tutorial/content "Dividing with negative numbers follows similar rules as multiplying with negative numbers. 

First of all, a negative number divided by a positive number gives a negative number. We can picture this rule as

$$
\begin{aligned}(-)\,÷\,(+)\,=\,(-).\end{aligned}
$$

For example, let's use this rule to find the value of $(-6) \div 2.$

Here, since we are dividing a negative number $\color{red}(-6)$ by a positive number ${\color{blue}(2)},$ the result is going to be negative:
![](images/b6/b64108fa03fc286ddcd04ac4cd7a9d77c1672d0ced66ebb1953c97afa5488533.svg)

Now, to compute the number that goes in the box, we divide $6$ by $2$ *without* any signs: $6 \div 2 = 3.$ So, we get

$$
{\color{red}(-6)} \div {\color{blue}2} = {\color{red} -3 }.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b92ac2e4-b983-5fd5-bc18-7dfb821497f0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8108 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "39aa10e9-422a-5c1c-b5b2-de119dcca067" :step/math-academy-id 77819 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065282}} {:db/id 17592186065282 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064357 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063941 :question/id #uuid "5b4f3b5f-2f0b-5178-9055-cf83a9885920" :question/math-academy-id "e-12972"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b434d0d5-bd04-554b-888e-df84e3961839" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049349}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064489} {:db/id 17592186064564} {:db/id 17592186064764} {:db/id 17592186442926} {:db/id 17592186442927} {:db/id 17592186442928} {:db/id 17592186442933} {:db/id 17592186442937}] :knowledge-point/title "Dividing a Negative Number by a Positive Number"} :step/id #uuid "46d3cb51-86b4-59d6-8a39-eab709bb05a3" :step/math-academy-id 77820 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065283}} {:db/id 17592186065283 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065417 :tutorial/content "A positive number divided by a negative number is also a negative number. We can picture this rule as

$$
\begin{aligned}(+)\,÷\,(-)\,=\,(-).\end{aligned}
$$

For instance, to find $8\div (-2),$ we have to divide a positive number $\color{blue}(8)$ by a negative one ${\color{red}(-2)}.$ So the result will be negative:
![](images/79/797eda7126fff569fccda2681c628f99f103057d7c5e23c1b65cb566b48ef203.svg)

Now, to compute the number that goes in the box, we divide $8$ by $2$ without any signs: $8 \div 2 = 4.$ So, we get

$$
{\color{blue}8} \div {\color{red}(-2)} = {\color{red}-4}.

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which expression represents the corresponding quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ in terms of the components of ![](images/31/31a4a301bddfd7435f188f76c1702beb7c2eea01a1b174d5195f321cfdef3103.png)" :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

Each entry $a_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term $a_{ij}x_i x_j$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =-1{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(1){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(1){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+-1{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}(-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}({x}_{1}-{x}_{2}) \\  & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162595 :question/id #uuid "ef8e1919-faae-510c-bb46-8c3989805365" :question/math-academy-id "q-93705" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186161986 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "328b0b77-f789-581e-a119-9823297666ae" :knowledge-point/title "Writing Down a Quadratic Form Given Its Matrix"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "37bed92b-f672-507f-908f-4180d60967a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}" :db/id 17592186355166} {:answer/id #uuid "7a4e148e-4cda-58e5-a8f8-33882e3c14d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}" :db/id 17592186355735} {:answer/id #uuid "bdd54d13-8fee-5d25-aa21-73e2fe837e31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}" :db/id 17592186356326} {:answer/id #uuid "ce4a3363-52f8-53e5-b467-965e5d801060" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}" :db/id 17592186356471} {:answer/id #uuid "de2c0735-3990-56ef-921f-e2e38cf38440" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-{x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}" :db/id 17592186356611}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "37bed92b-f672-507f-908f-4180d60967a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}" :db/id 17592186355166} :answer-field/id #uuid "24c65efe-f0dc-5833-85bd-c0e38f31a3b2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186356981}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in terms of the components of $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =1{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(-2){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(-2){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(-2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}

A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in terms of the components of $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =2{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+0{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+1{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+(-2){x}_{2}{x}_{2}+0{x}_{2}{x}_{3}+0{x}_{3}{x}_{1}+0{x}_{3}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}{x}_{3} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & {x}_{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & {x}_{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}(2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})+{x}_{3}(2{x}_{3}) \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{x}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186357656 :question/id #uuid "fee716f7-a185-58ac-8ee8-36859424ee03" :question/math-academy-id "q-94105" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186161986 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "328b0b77-f789-581e-a119-9823297666ae" :knowledge-point/title "Writing Down a Quadratic Form Given Its Matrix"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "074bc0a8-4ace-5935-8132-e8516c14bc11" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{3}+3{x}_{3}^{2}" :db/id 17592186354727} {:answer/id #uuid "0c35860c-44ad-5b5c-89ff-8920a976c568" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{3}" :db/id 17592186354776} {:answer/id #uuid "29a555f5-45bd-56ad-b133-4ea913d8ef19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2{x}_{2}^{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{3}+3{x}_{3}^{2}" :db/id 17592186355011} {:answer/id #uuid "6211823f-d038-5a7f-841f-e14f57f1ed54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}-3{x}_{3}^{2}" :db/id 17592186355538} {:answer/id #uuid "aa727819-380a-594d-a4bd-a5f02c1e6dbc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{3}+3{x}_{3}^{2}" :db/id 17592186356172}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "074bc0a8-4ace-5935-8132-e8516c14bc11" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{3}+3{x}_{3}^{2}" :db/id 17592186354727} :answer-field/id #uuid "135db05c-789b-5517-a595-77d2c4b006a8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186356952}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+(-2){x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\  & +\,(-2){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must split the coefficient of $-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ between the entries 

$$
{a}_{12}={a}_{21}=\frac{(-4)}{2}=-2
$$

of our matrix. So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, $a=2$ and $b=-2.$ Finally, 

$$
a+b=2+(-2)=0.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186357659 :question/id #uuid "5a9d7088-7e39-5869-b0a9-78e9adad33f9" :question/math-academy-id "q-94113"} {:db/id 17592186357660 :question/id #uuid "6a58c19a-d8e2-5b8b-a8c1-6d0a7f511f7e" :question/math-academy-id "q-94115" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186161987 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "eb93c0ea-26d9-5190-9677-b8c7eb6f7ef1" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "02a9e9a8-3c46-5c6f-a0b9-c715263b46fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186354679} {:answer/id #uuid "70d8b306-7d64-5a53-bf09-1fcafe21fe9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186355662} {:answer/id #uuid "cacc7a23-abd5-5d11-b9dd-14002a05348f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186356433} {:answer/id #uuid "cc6a54ea-970f-5bca-8ce6-3a18756c0f41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186356448} {:answer/id #uuid "d57fe9de-2cd2-5256-980e-2266baf495ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186356534}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "cacc7a23-abd5-5d11-b9dd-14002a05348f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186356433} :answer-field/id #uuid "8a785e93-2dfe-5d3a-8afd-c6a0e1ac5840" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186357165}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+1{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\  & +\,1{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+(-2){x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must split the coefficient of $2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ between the entries 

$$
{a}_{12}={a}_{21}=\frac{2}{2}=1
$$

of our matrix. So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, $b=1$ and $c=-2.$ Finally, 

$$
b+c=1-2=-1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186357661 :question/id #uuid "9072a42a-e341-5217-87b1-4c9dd2071c09" :question/math-academy-id "q-94116"} {:db/id 17592186357662 :question/id #uuid "975a9fdb-6284-526d-91e7-201bd08f5d18" :question/math-academy-id "q-94117"} {:db/id 17592186357663 :question/id #uuid "b751a90c-cbe5-589a-aef5-36f0a41388ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-94120" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186161987 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "eb93c0ea-26d9-5190-9677-b8c7eb6f7ef1" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26e98748-b388-5506-aac1-9e30f72043d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186354991} {:answer/id #uuid "3dd9af0b-3c0e-55a4-a669-bcadc34c08b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186355216} {:answer/id #uuid "4978df42-b859-52a6-ba63-1a347384a158" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186355314} {:answer/id #uuid "e34d7105-1d3f-5ec1-968a-d5410c870152" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186356653} {:answer/id #uuid "e64af5fe-d6ac-5ec1-be75-b923dae80e06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186356678}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "e34d7105-1d3f-5ec1-968a-d5410c870152" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186356653} :answer-field/id #uuid "57a91600-a00a-59db-b63e-edcd7437f52e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186357067}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$$

$$

$$

$$

[{:db/id 17592186162851 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163226 :tutorial/content "Given a bilinear form $B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ such that 

$$
B:\Bbb R^n \times \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R
$$

and the corresponding $n \times n$ matrix is *symmetric*, we can define the so-called **quadratic form** by substituting $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}$ as follows:

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})= B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}).
$$

 

Notice that the new expression depends only on $\mathbf{x}.$ So, a quadratic form is a function 

$$
Q:\Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R.
$$

In matrix notation, a quadratic form  can be given as 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x},
$$

 

where $A$ is a symmetric matrix. It's called the **matrix of the quadratic form**. 

**Watch out!** By definition, the matrix of a quadratic form must be *symmetric*.

For example, given the bilinear form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

the corresponding quadratic form is then
$Q( \mathbf{x})=B( \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}).$
Explicitly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({x}_{1},{x}_{2}) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

**Note**: In a quadratic form, all terms must be of degree two (considered as polynomials in the variables $x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n$). That's the reason we call it *quadratic*." :tutorial/id #uuid "f35d3e6c-6386-5c92-91c9-05fe3d888a47" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4884 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid That's the reason we call it *quadratic*." :tutorial/id #uuid "f35d3e6c-6386-5c92-91c9-05fe3d888a47" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4884 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "79f6f6cd-00ca-545a-aec0-257cfc16bf2b" :step/math-academy-id 30535 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162866}} {:db/id 17592186163226 :tutorial/content "Given a bilinear form $B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ such that 

$$
B:\Bbb R^n \times \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R
$$

and the corresponding $n \times n$ matrix is *symmetric*, we can define the so-called **quadratic form** by substituting $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}$ as follows:

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})= B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}).
$$

 

Notice that the new expression depends only on $\mathbf{x}.$ So, a quadratic form is a function 

$$
Q:\Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R.
$$

In matrix notation, a quadratic form  can be given as 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x},
$$

 

where $A$ is a symmetric matrix. It's called the **matrix of the quadratic form**. 

**Watch out!** By definition, the matrix of a quadratic form must be *symmetric*.

For example, given the bilinear form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

the corresponding quadratic form is then
$Q( \mathbf{x})=B( \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}).$
Explicitly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({x}_{1},{x}_{2}) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

**Note**: In a quadratic form, all terms must be of degree two (considered as polynomials in the variables $x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n$). eigenvalue $\lambda = 9?$" :question/worked-solution "For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda = 9,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ is a vector $\mathbf{v}$ such that 

$$
(A - 9I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
\quad \textrm{and} \quad
(A - 9I)^3 \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}.
$$

Notice that $A$ must be a $14 \times 14$ matrix.

- Since the rank of $(A-9I)^3$ equals $9,$ then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-9I)^3 = 14-9 = 5.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A - 9I)^3 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-9I)^3$ of dimension $5$ in $\mathbb{R}^{14}.$

- Since the rank of $(A-9I)^4$ equals $7,$  then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-9I)^4 = 14-7 = 7.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A - 9I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-9I)^4$ of dimension $7$ in $\mathbb{R}^{14}.$

Since $\text{Null}(A-9I)^3$ is a subspace of dimension $5$ in $\text{Null}(A-9I)^4$, which is a subspace of dimension $7,$ our basis can contain only $2$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(A-9I)^4$ but not in $\text{Null}(A-9I)^3.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-9I)^4 - \text{nullity}(A-9I)^3 = 7-5=2
$$

In the characteristic polynomial

$$
p(\lambda) = (1+\lambda) (4-\lambda)^3(\lambda-1)^5,
$$

we see that the root $\lambda = 1$ has multiplicity $5.$ So the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1$ is $5.$

However, there are only $3$ eigenvectors corresponding to  the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1,$ so the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1$ is $3.$

Therefore, the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ corresponding to $\lambda = 1$ is $5-3=2.$"} {:db/id 17592186049408} {:db/id 17592186050376} {:db/id 17592186050857} {:db/id 17592186176247 :question/id #uuid "3cb467c0-ea77-596f-b372-4352d634576f" :question/math-academy-id "q-109740" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186175984 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dfc9161a-5f14-5c16-afb0-832f81f30be4" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of Rank Greater Than One"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f6bab197-73af-5629-bd73-9a2539823707" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186173741} {:answer/id #uuid "fa1ab9c9-85f4-531d-b3a7-bea26e2d3c0c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186173742} {:answer/id #uuid "3c42c8d8-a86c-5a0e-9310-317060bb58bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186173743} {:answer/id #uuid "5029f1b5-3ff3-57ee-bad8-a1511f8c44c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186173744} {:answer/id #uuid "69acfa87-eb10-5b78-aa51-34879b469042" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186173745}] :answer-field/id #uuid "575ab359-7284-535c-aa54-794bcba6804d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186173740}] :question/problem "Suppose that a matrix $D$ has characteristic polynomial $p(λ) = λ^{3}(4 - λ)^{2}(7 - λ)^{6}$, and for the eigenvalue $λ = 0$, there are exactly $2$ eigenvectors. (A - \pi I)^3 \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A-\pi I)^3$ has dimension $4.$ This means that the solutions to $(A - \pi I)^3 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace of dimension $4.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A-\pi I)^4$ has dimension $6.$ This means that the solutions to $(A - \pi I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace of dimension $6.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(A-\pi I)^3$ is a subspace of dimension $4$ in $\text{Null}(A-\pi I)^4$, which is a subspace of dimension $6,$ our basis can contain only $2$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(A-\pi I)^4$ but not in $\text{Null}(A-\pi I)^3.$

Therefore, there will be

\text{nullity}(A-\pi I)^4 - \text{nullity}(A-\pi I)^3 = 6-4=2
$$
